title: Connecting communities through collaboration in Rwanda
summary: This summer, a team of Jacobs volunteers traveled to Karambo, Rwanda, to work with Fika and the local community on the construction of a suspended pedestrian bridge that will improve access to schools, healthcare, markets and essential services for thousands of residents.
body_markdown:
Rwanda is known as the Land of a Thousand Hills, and nowhere was that more evident than in Karambo. Surrounded by lush green valleys, terraced hillsides and winding footpaths, the community's beauty was striking. Yet the same landscape that makes this region so remarkable can also create barriers to opportunity, especially during the rainy season when rivers become difficult and dangerous to cross.


This summer, a team of Jacobs volunteers traveled the area to work with Fika (formerly Bridges to Prosperity) and the local community on the construction of a suspended pedestrian bridge creating a vital connection to education, healthcare, markets and economic opportunity. For thousands of people who will use it, the bridge represents safer journeys, greater access and new possibilities for the future.


The project embodied collaboration at every stage with community members, Fika staff and Jacobs team members working side-by-side throughout the build, sharing knowledge, solving challenges together and learning from one another.


That spirit of connection extended far beyond the construction site. Before arriving in Rwanda, team members spent months learning about the country's history, language, culture and traditions. Once on the ground, that learning continued through visits local businesses, conversations with community members, participation in cultural activities and a visit to Kigali's Genocide Memorial. Every interaction offered an opportunity to better understand the resilience, warmth and pride that define Rwanda and its people.


Picture credit: Envision


One of the most memorable moments came during a visit to G.S. Karambo School, where nearly 1,000 students welcomed the team with songs and dancing. For many participants, seeing the children who would benefit from safer access to education brought the purpose of the project into sharp focus.


The project also focused on creating a lasting legacy. Throughout the build, community maintenance ambassadors received training and support to help care for the bridge long after construction was complete. Together, the team was doing more than building a bridge — it was strengthening local capability and long-term ownership.
"I have gained a lot of skills here; I started out as a site assistant but through this experience, I can now work as a skilled mason. I didn’t know how to tighten screws or build with stone but now I have mastered it,” said local resident Mutamaruka J. Pierra.


When inauguration day arrived there was singing, dancing, laughter and a sense of collective pride as community members crossed the bridge for the first time. Children raced from one side to the other, eager to experience the connection they had watched take shape over the previous two weeks.


For the Jacobs team, the most enduring memories were not the cables, tools or engineering milestones. They were the friendships formed, the lessons exchanged and the opportunity to work alongside a community determined to invest in its own future.


-


> I joined the project wanting to make a meaningful impact, but what I experienced was far greater than I imagined. Working alongside the community, learning from Rwandan culture and building relationships across languages and backgrounds showed me that lasting impact comes from both the bridge we constructed and the connections we created along the way.


Richard Rowe-Roberts


Support team Member
